bag.bluemountain.text: Only coffee certified by the Jamaica Commodities Regulatory Authority can be sold under this name.
bag.decaf.name: Decaf
bag.decaf.text: US standards require at least 97% of the caffeine to be removed; the EU standard is 99.9% caffeine-free by mass. Ludwig Roselius invented the first commercial process in 1903.
bag.espresso.name: Espresso
bag.espresso.text: Coffee brewed by forcing hot, pressurised water through finely ground coffee. Angelo Moriondo of Turin patented a steam-driven coffee machine in 1884.
bag.gesha.name: Geisha or Gesha
bag.gesha.text: A coffee variety that originated in Ethiopia. Panama made it famous at auction.
bag.instant.name: Instant
bag.instant.text: Nestlé launched Nescafé in Switzerland on 1 April 1938, made to use up a coffee surplus.
bag.java.name: Java
bag.java.text: Coffee from the Indonesian island of Java. By 1719 the Dutch East India Company could supply Europe's demand with "Java coffee".
bag.kona.name: Kona
bag.kona.text: Coffee from the Kona district of Hawaii, where Samuel Ruggles brought Brazilian cuttings in 1828.
bag.turkish.link: What unfiltered coffee means for your health
bag.turkish.name: Turkish coffee
bag.turkish.text: Very finely ground coffee, brought just to the boil in a cezve and served unfiltered, with the grounds left in the cup. UNESCO listed Turkish coffee culture and tradition in 2013.

faq.a2: The store shows its own crossed-out "was" price. We show it in amber and don't count it as a drop: a "was" price is the store's claim, our price history is the proof.
faq.a3: From each roaster's and tea house's own online shop, as a buyer in the US, the UK or the EU sees them. Shipping isn't included. Check the final price on the store's site before you buy.
faq.a4: Some stores convert their prices for other countries. A converted price can move with the exchange rate alone, so we count it as a drop only when the store's price in its own currency dropped too.
faq.a5: No. CoffeeProof is independent: it reads prices and links to the store. Purchases happen on the store's own site.

glossary.arabica.d: The coffee species most specialty coffee comes from; it grows best at altitude.
glossary.black.d: Tea whose leaves are fully oxidised.
glossary.blend.d: Coffees from several origins, mixed by the roaster for a steady taste.
glossary.camellia.d: The tea plant. Black, green, oolong, white and pu-erh teas all come from it.
glossary.chai.d: Tea brewed with spices, or a spice blend for it; usually based on black tea.
glossary.decaf.d: Coffee with most of its caffeine removed; US rules ask for at least 97%.
glossary.espresso_roast.d: A coffee its roaster roasts or recommends for espresso.
glossary.gesha.d: A coffee variety first found in Ethiopia, known from Panama's auction records.
glossary.green.d: Tea heated soon after picking, so the leaves don't oxidise.
glossary.herbal.d: An infusion of herbs, flowers, fruit or roots, such as rooibos or chamomile; not from the tea plant.
glossary.honey.d: The skin is removed but some of the sticky fruit is left on the bean while it dries.
glossary.lowest30.d: A real drop with no cheaper day in the last 30.
glossary.matcha.d: Shade-grown green tea ground into a powder and whisked into water.
glossary.natural.d: The whole coffee cherry dries with the bean inside, before the fruit is removed.
glossary.oolong.d: Tea whose leaves are partly oxidised, between green and black.
glossary.per_unit.d: The price for the same weight, to compare bags of different sizes: per kg for coffee, per 100 g for tea.
glossary.puerh.d: A tea from Yunnan, China, often pressed into cakes and aged.
glossary.real_drop.d: Today's price under the usual price, by our own price history.
glossary.roast_level.d: How long and how hot the beans were roasted: light, medium or dark.
glossary.robusta.d: A hardier coffee species with more caffeine, often used in espresso blends and instant coffee.
glossary.single_origin.d: Coffee from one country, region or farm, named after where it grew.
glossary.store_sale.d: A price the store shows against its own crossed-out "was" price; we don't count it as a drop.
glossary.usual.d: The highest price a size sold for on at least 7 of the last 30 days.
glossary.washed.d: The fruit is removed from the bean before drying.
glossary.white.d: Buds and young leaves, withered and dried with little handling.
glossary.whole_bean.d: Beans as roasted, or ground for a brew method.

guides.title: Coffee guides
guides.write.li1: Every claim links to its source. Public health agencies, peer-reviewed research and named reference works, listed at the end of each guide.
guides.write.li2: Links, not causes. Most coffee research is observational. When a study shows a link, we call it a link.
guides.write.li3: Not medical advice. The health guide is general information. Talk to your doctor about your own caffeine limits.
guides.write.p: The same rule as our prices: don't take a claim on trust, show where it comes from.
health.bad.bones.p: The BMJ review found a higher fracture risk in women, though not in men.
health.bad.cholesterol.p: French press and Turkish coffee keep compounds called diterpenes, about 30 times more than filtered coffee. They can raise cholesterol.
health.bad.hot.p: IARC classes drinks hotter than 65 °C as probably carcinogenic. Give your cup a minute.
health.bad.note: The research is about coffee itself, not the sugar, syrups and pastries that often come with it.
health.bad.p: None of this means coffee is bad for you. It means there are limits worth knowing.
health.bad.pregnancy.p: High intake in pregnancy is linked with low birth weight, preterm birth and pregnancy loss. EFSA's level is 200 mg a day; check with your doctor.
health.bad.sleep.p: In a 2013 study, 400 mg of caffeine taken six hours before bed cut sleep by more than an hour, and people didn't notice. The AASM, which published it, says caffeine should generally be avoided after 5 p.m.
health.bad.toomuch.p: Signs include jitters, anxiety, a fast heart rate and poor sleep. Toxic effects such as seizures can come from about 1,200 mg taken quickly: less than half a teaspoon of pure caffeine.
health.calc.h: How much caffeine is in your day?
health.careful.children: Children and teens: EFSA suggests 3 mg per kg of body weight a day as a safe level.
health.careful.fractures: Women at risk of fractures or with osteoporosis: the BMJ authors suggest keeping coffee to a minimum.
health.careful.pregnant: Pregnant, trying or breastfeeding: the FDA says to ask your provider whether to limit caffeine; EFSA's level is 200 mg a day.
health.careful.sensitive: People who feel caffeine strongly: how sensitive people are, and how fast they clear caffeine, varies widely. If you cut back, go gradually: withdrawal isn't dangerous, but it can be unpleasant.
health.desc: How much caffeine is too much, what a big 2017 review linked coffee with, unfiltered coffee and cholesterol, and a caffeine calculator, every claim linked to its source.
health.filter.filtered.p: A filtered cup has about a thirtieth of the diterpenes of an unfiltered one.
health.filter.p: How you brew changes what ends up in the cup. Harvard Health suggests saving unfiltered coffee for rare occasions and keeping to fewer than five cups a day on average.
health.filter.unfiltered.p: About 30 times more diterpenes than filtered coffee.
health.good.cancer.p: In 2016 the WHO's cancer agency, IARC, found no conclusive evidence that drinking coffee causes cancer, and lists it as "not classifiable".
health.good.heart.p: The same review linked coffee with less cardiovascular disease and fewer deaths from it.
health.good.life.p: Coffee drinkers had a lower risk of dying from any cause, with the biggest drop at three to four cups a day.
health.good.liver.p: Coffee went with a lower risk of liver conditions, including liver cancer.
health.good.note: These come from observational studies, so they show links, not causes. The BMJ authors say they can't recommend starting coffee for your health.
health.good.p: A 2017 BMJ umbrella review looked at more than 200 meta-analyses. Coffee came out more likely to benefit health than to harm it.
health.lede: The good, the not so good, and how much caffeine is too much. Every claim links to its source.
health.myth.cancer.a: Myth. IARC's 2016 review found no conclusive evidence and lists coffee as "not classifiable". Drinks hotter than 65 °C are a separate warning.
health.myth.cancer.q: "Coffee is on the list of things that cause cancer."
health.myth.decaf.a: Myth. US rules require at least 97% of the caffeine to be removed, so a little is left.
health.myth.espresso.a: Myth. A 1 oz shot has about 63 mg; an 8 oz cup of brewed coffee about 96 mg. Espresso is stronger per sip, not per serving.
health.myth.espresso.q: "A shot of espresso has more caffeine than a mug of coffee."
health.myth.limit.a: Fact. That's the level the FDA and EFSA use. Pregnancy has a lower one: 200 mg a day.
health.myth.limit.q: "Up to 400 mg a day is fine for most healthy adults."
health.note: This guide is general information, not medical advice. If you have a health condition, take medication or are pregnant, talk to your doctor about caffeine.
health.page_title: Coffee and your health: what the research says — CoffeeProof
health.short.li1: For most healthy adults, up to 400 mg of caffeine a day isn't linked to harmful effects. The FDA puts that at about two to three 12 oz cups of coffee.
health.short.li2: Pregnant or breastfeeding? EFSA's level is 200 mg a day. Ask your doctor too.
health.short.li3: In a big 2017 review, three to four cups a day went with a lower risk of several diseases. Those studies can't prove coffee is the cause.

Our crawler is shared with our sister sites: it calls itself wheyproofbot, signs its requests and follows each store's robots.txt. More about the crawler.

moment.1554.text: Two Arab merchants open the city's first coffeehouse, in Tahtakale.
moment.1580.text: The botanist Prospero Alpini brings coffee to Venice from Egypt.
moment.1671.text: The goatherd legend first appears in writing, set in Arabia Felix.
moment.1696.text: The Dutch governor in Malabar sends Yemeni arabica seedlings to Batavia, now Jakarta.
moment.1711.text: The first Java coffee is shipped to Europe.
moment.1720.text: Gabriel de Clieu brings coffee seedlings to the island.
moment.1727.text: The country's first coffee plantation starts from seeds smuggled in from French Guiana.
moment.1828.text: Samuel Ruggles brings Brazilian cuttings to the Kona district.
moment.1884.text: Angelo Moriondo patents a steam-driven "instantaneous" coffee machine.
moment.1902.text: Luigi Bezzera patents improvements to the machine. Desiderio Pavoni buys the patent in 1903.
moment.1903.text: Ludwig Roselius invents a way to take the caffeine out of coffee. It's patented in 1906.
moment.1938.text: Nestlé launches Nescafé, made to use up a coffee surplus after Brazil's prices fell.
moment.1945.text: Achille Gaggia develops the lever-driven espresso machine.
moment.2004.text: The first Geisha ever auctioned sells for $21 a pound.
moment.2013.text: Turkish coffee culture and tradition joins UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
moment.2019.text: An Elida Estate Gesha fetches $1,029 a pound at the Best of Panama auction.
moment.late1400s.text: Coffee drinking is first recorded, among Sufi communities.

privacy.cloudflare.p: Our pages are delivered through Cloudflare, which handles visitors' requests, including their IP addresses, to deliver and protect the site.
privacy.cookies.p: We set a cookie only when you use a control that needs one: the theme, the watchlist and the comparison. See the cookie policy.
privacy.log.p: Like most websites, our server keeps a log of the requests it answers: the IP address, the time, the page asked for (including what is in its address, such as a search or a calculator's numbers), the browser's user agent and the page you came from. We use it to keep the site running and safe, and it is deleted after 90 days. The server is in Frankfurt, Germany.
privacy.none.p: There are no accounts, no sign-up and no newsletter, and our pages carry no analytics or advertising trackers.
privacy.photos.p: Product photos load from each store's own image server (for most stores, Shopify's), so your browser asks that server for them. Our font is served from our own server.
privacy.rights.p: You can ask us what we hold about you, and to delete it. In the access log we can only find entries by IP address and time.
privacy.who.p: CoffeeProof (coffeeproof.org). Questions about this policy: support@wheyproof.com.

story.brazil.text: Brazil's first coffee plantation dates from 1727, when Lt. Col. Francisco de Melo Palheta smuggled seeds in from French Guiana. Two centuries later, a coffee surplus left by Brazil's falling prices led Nestlé to develop Nescafé, launched in 1938.
story.brazil.title: Brazil's first plantation
story.istanbul.text: According to the Ottoman chronicler İbrahim Peçevi, two Arab merchants, from Aleppo and Damascus, opened the city's first coffeehouse in Tahtakale in 1554. In 2013 UNESCO added Turkish coffee culture and tradition to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.
story.istanbul.title: Istanbul's first coffeehouse
story.jamaica.text: Coffee was introduced to Jamaica in 1728. Today only coffee certified by the Jamaica Commodities Regulatory Authority can be sold as Jamaica Blue Mountain, named for mountains that rise to 2,256 m.
story.jamaica.title: Coffee comes to Jamaica
story.java.text: In 1696 the Dutch governor in Malabar, India, sent seedlings of Yemeni arabica to Batavia, now Jakarta. Floods killed the first batch, and a second shipment followed in 1699. In 1711 the Dutch East India Company sent the first Java coffee to Europe.
story.java.title: Java coffee sails for Europe
story.kona.text: In 1828 the Reverend Samuel Ruggles brought coffee to the Kona district of Hawaii, from Brazilian cuttings.
story.kona.title: Brazilian cuttings in Hawaii
story.martinique.text: Gabriel de Clieu brought coffee seedlings to the island of Martinique in 1720. From there coffee spread to Saint-Domingue, Mexico and other Caribbean islands.
story.martinique.title: Seedlings reach the Caribbean
story.panama.text: The Geisha variety originated in Ethiopia and reached Panama from Costa Rica. The first Geisha ever auctioned, a washed lot from Hacienda La Esmeralda in 2004, sold for $21 a pound. In 2019 a natural Gesha from Elida Estate fetched $1,029 a pound at the Best of Panama auction.
story.panama.title: Geisha and the auction records
story.venice.text: The botanist Prospero Alpini brought coffee to Venice from Egypt in 1580. In 1645 the city opened mainland Europe's first coffeehouse.
story.venice.title: Coffee reaches mainland Europe
story.yemen.text: Coffee drinking is first recorded in the late 15th century, among Sufi communities in Yemen. There's no confirmed evidence of coffee as a drink before then. The famous goatherd legend came much later: its first written version, from 1671, is set in Arabia Felix, in the south of the Arabian peninsula.
story.yemen.title: The first coffee drinkers we know of
terms.badges.p: A badge is our reading of our own price history, not a statement by the store.
terms.buying.p: CoffeeProof isn't a store. A purchase, its delivery and any return are between you and the store.
terms.changes.p: We may change the site and these terms; the date at the top says when they last changed. Questions: contact.
terms.guides.p: They are general information, not medical advice.
terms.names.p: Product names and photos belong to their owners and are shown to identify the products.
terms.prices.p: We read prices once a day from each store's own site. The store's site has the final word on the price, the stock and the shipping; check it before you buy.
